spec.full_target:
Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
spec.conclusion: dim_H(E x [0,1]) = dim_H(E) + 1, with the Euclidean metric under Eucl(n) x R = Eucl(n+1), including n=0.

definitions.type: family of Euclidean metric spaces indexed by natural numbers
definitions.definition: For each natural number m, Eucl(m)=R^m with distance between x and y equal to (sum_{j=1}^m (x_j-y_j)^2)^(1/2). Eucl(0) is the singleton empty tuple. Identify Eucl(m) x R with Eucl(m+1) by concatenating coordinates; its distance is sqrt(dist(x,y)^2+|t-u|^2), throughout, including m=0.

definitions.type: extended nonnegative diameter of a subset of a metric space
definitions.definition: diam(A)=sup{dist(x,y):x,y in A}, with diameter of the empty set zero; it may be infinity. In a native extended metric space the same quantity is ediam(A). At finite diameter it is identified with its nonnegative real value.

definitions.type: unnormalized Hausdorff contents and Hausdorff measures of Euclidean sets
definitions.definition:
For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put

\[
H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
 A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
\qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
\]

Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This

definitions.type: native Hausdorff measure notation for real exponents on extended metric spaces
definitions.definition: muH[a] denotes Mathlib MeasureTheory.Measure.hausdorffMeasure a, constructed as the metric measure from the set cost ediam(U)^a, using the Borel measurable structure; its construction is native mkMetric (fun r => r^a). This definition asserts no comparison with H. Native infinite sums and integrals take values in [0,infinity].

definitions.definition: dimH(A) is the native Mathlib Hausdorff dimension: sup over nonnegative real a such that muH[a](A)=infinity of a, as an element of [0,infinity], with supremum of the empty family zero. The measurable structure used here is Borel.

definitions.type: Hausdorff dimension of a Euclidean set
definitions.definition: dim_H(A) is the usual Hausdorff dimension, represented by dimH(A) on its Euclidean metric. Its meaning is the supremum of nonnegative exponents a for which the native Hausdorff measure muH[a](A) is infinite, with supremum of the empty family zero. Values lie in [0,infinity]. Its equivalence with the critical exponent of the supplied unnormalized covering measure is a proof obligation, not an original hypothesis.

definitions.type: Lebesgue measure on the real line and nonnegative Lebesgue integration
definitions.definition: lambda is Lebesgue length measure on R, with its Lebesgue measurable structure. Integrals below are nonnegative Lebesgue integrals valued in [0,infinity]; integration over a measurable set uses the restricted measure. For a set J, 1_J(t) is 1 when t belongs to J and 0 otherwise. locals.declaration: Fix an arbitrary natural number m.
Fix an arbitrary subset A of Eucl(m).
Fix an arbitrary real s, and assume L1: s>0.

argument.text: Fix m,A and s>0 (L1). Apply M002 to Eucl(m), with its Euclidean extended metric and Borel measurable structure, exponent s and set A. At each finite positive scale its inner infimum is exactly H^s_delta(A): every countable cover is enumerable by naturals, with empty padding if needed, and each nonempty-member inner supremum is just its diameter to power s, whereas an empty member has cost zero. At a finite scale all nonempty admissible diameters are finite, so ediam and the usual diameter agree. The additional native scale infinity does not change the outer supremum: its admissible covers include those at every finite scale, so its infimum is no larger. Every positive finite extended scale is a positive real scale. Thus M002 gives muH[s](A)=sup_delta H^s_delta(A)=H^s(A).

Use F001. The native dimension dimH(A) is dim_H(A) by the representation in D006 and is nonnegative because it is a supremum in [0,infinity]. Regard s as a nonnegative real, using s>0. M003 gives infinity when s<dim_H(A); M004 gives zero when dim_H(A)<s. If H^s(A)=0, F001 makes the native measure zero and hence unequal to infinity, so M005 gives dim_H(A)<=s. If H^s(A)=infinity, F001 and M006 give s<=dim_H(A). These conclusions hold for the arbitrary Euclidean dimension m and set A, including infinite dimension values. Discharge L1 and universally quantify: all the asserted clauses follow.

locals.declaration: For the finite-content assertion, take arbitrary s>0.
Take an arbitrary scale delta>0.
Choose L>0 with E contained in [-L,L]^n, whose existence is F001.
Define C=(2L+2)^n.
Let 0<h<=1 vary towards zero.
Fix an arbitrary exponent a>n.

argument.text: H002 gives compactness. The open balls of radius delta/2 centered at points of E form an open cover; a finite subcover has diameters at most delta and finite s-cost. Thus H^s_delta(E) is finite for arbitrary s>0,delta>0. Also the increasing boxes (-k,k)^n, for positive integer k, cover Eucl(n). A finite subcover of E places E in some [-L,L]^n with L>0. This proves the required existence of a bounding box. Nonnegativity of D follows from N001.

produces.statement: There exists a real L_b>0 such that E is contained in [-L_b,L_b]^n.
For every s_b>0 and delta_b>0, H^{s_b}_{delta_b}(E)<infinity.

argument.text: For the branch L1: n>=1, choose the bounding box from F001. Subdivide each coordinate interval [-L,L] into ceil(2L/h) pieces of length at most h, where 0<h<=1. Taking products covers the box by at most (2L/h+1)^n <= C h^(-n) cubes, where C=(2L+2)^n. Each cube has Euclidean diameter at most sqrt(n) h. Hence for any a>n the total a-cost is at most C n^(a/2) h^(a-n), tending to zero as h decreases to zero; the maximum diameter tends to zero as well. For each fixed positive scale these covers eventually satisfy its diameter bound and have arbitrarily small cost. Thus H^a(E)=0. N001 gives D<=a for all a>n, hence D<=n (otherwise choose a strictly between n and D; if D=infinity any a>n contradicts D<=a). Discharge L1 to obtain the conditional branch conclusion.

For the branch L2: n=0, H001 and the fact that Eucl(0) has just its empty tuple give E=Eucl(0), a singleton. For every positive exponent its one-member singleton cover has diameter and cost zero at every scale. N001 therefore gives D<=a for every a>0; together with nonnegativity this is D=0. Discharge L2. Since a natural n is either zero or at least one, F003 and this branch yield 0<=D<=n, with the stated singleton assertion when n=0. F002 supplies the finite-content clause.

argument.text: For any a>1 and each positive integer k, the k closed intervals [j/k,(j+1)/k], 0<=j<k, cover I. Their diameters are 1/k, and their total a-cost is k*(1/k)^a=k^(1-a), tending to zero as k tends to infinity. At any fixed scale the diameter bound holds for all sufficiently large k. Hence H^a_delta(I)=0 at every positive scale and H^a(I)=0 for every a>1.

Fix delta>0 and an arbitrary countable delta-cover T of I. Ignore empty terms by K={i:T_i nonempty}, and set rho_i=diam(T_i)<=delta. For epsilon>0 the bounded nonempty real set T_i has infimum and supremum, with sup T_i-inf T_i=rho_i. Define the open interval J_i=(inf T_i-epsilon*2^(-i-2),sup T_i+epsilon*2^(-i-2)); it contains T_i and has length rho_i+epsilon*2^(-i-1). These intervals cover I. Countable subadditivity of Lebesgue length, lambda(I)=1, and the geometric sum over K bounded by the full sum over N give 1<=sum_i lambda(J_i)<=sum_i rho_i+epsilon. If sum_i rho_i is infinite the claim is immediate; otherwise letting epsilon decrease to zero gives sum_i rho_i>=1. This holds for the arbitrary cover and scale.

argument.text: For arbitrary 0<s<1, retain delta and T, K, rho. For 0<rho_i<=delta the negative exponent s-1 gives rho_i^(s-1)>=delta^(s-1), hence rho_i^s>=delta^(s-1)*rho_i. When rho_i=0 the same inequality is 0>=0, since s>0. Sum the inequalities and apply F002: sum_i rho_i^s>=delta^(s-1)*sum_i rho_i>=delta^(s-1). The same holds with empty terms contributing zero. Take the infimum over the arbitrary delta-covers to obtain H^s_delta(I)>=delta^(s-1). Since s-1<0 this lower bound tends to infinity as delta decreases to zero; consequently H^s(I)=infinity for every 0<s<1. This also records the coverwise bound required in the output.

argument.text: First treat L1: n=0. N002 gives E=Eucl(0), a singleton, and D=0. Coordinate concatenation identifies F isometrically with I. Push the interval partitions used in N003 into F; the same diameters and costs give H^a(F)=0 for every a>1. By N001, dim_H(F)<=1=D+1. Discharge L1 and retain this branch conclusion.

Assume L2: n>=1. Fix q>D. N002 implies q>0, and N001 gives H^q(E)=0. Thus for any 0<r<=1 and epsilon>0 the infimum H^q_r(E)=0 supplies a countable r-cover with cost below epsilon/2. Discard its empty members. Each remaining zero-diameter set is a singleton. Enumerate such members by their original natural indices i and replace the i-th by a ball centered at that singleton, of positive diameter at most r and with q-cost <epsilon*2^(-i-2). Such balls exist in Eucl(n) because n>=1: their diameters are twice their positive radii, which may be made arbitrarily small since q>0. The replacement costs sum to at most epsilon/2 (indeed the strict bounds have that geometric majorant); with the initial strict epsilon/2 bound the final cost is <epsilon. Unchanged positive-diameter members already have diameter <=r. This proves existence of the positive-diameter cover needed next.

argument.text: Choose U as in F002 and put r_i=diam(U_i), N_i=ceil(1/r_i). The N_i intervals [j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i], 0<=j<N_i, cover I and have length 1/N_i<=r_i. Since r_i<=1, N_i<=1/r_i+1<=2/r_i. The products of U_i with these intervals form a countable cover of F: a countable union of finite families is countable. By the Euclidean product distance, each product diameter is at most sqrt(2)*r_i. Thus their total (q+1)-cost is at most sum_i N_i*(sqrt(2)*r_i)^(q+1) <= 2*(sqrt(2))^(q+1)*sum_i r_i^q < 2*(sqrt(2))^(q+1)*epsilon.

argument.text: Fix s>0 and delta>0 and put c=H^s_delta(E). N002 proves c finite. Take an arbitrary countable delta-cover V of F, and restrict to its nonempty-member indices K, a subset of N. Put rho_i=diam(V_i), A_i=the first-coordinate projection of V_i, and B_i=the last-coordinate projection. By the Euclidean distance formula each coordinate projection is 1-Lipschitz: dist of projected points is no more than dist of the original points. Consequently diam(A_i)<=rho_i and diam(B_i)<=rho_i<=delta. Every B_i is nonempty and bounded; its infimum and supremum are finite and sup B_i-inf B_i<=rho_i. No measurability of V_i,A_i or B_i is asserted or needed.

argument.text: For epsilon>0 define eta_i=epsilon*2^(-i-1)/(1+rho_i^s)>0 and J_i=(inf B_i-eta_i/2,sup B_i+eta_i/2). F001 makes these finite open intervals containing B_i, with length at most rho_i+eta_i. Define f_i(t)=rho_i^s*1_{J_i}(t). Each coefficient is finite and nonnegative, each J_i is open, and therefore every f_i is Lebesgue measurable, hence almost everywhere measurable for lambda restricted to I. The family has countable index set K.

That index lies in K, x belongs to A_i, and t belongs to B_i subset J_i by F002. These A_i have diameter <=rho_i<=delta by F001, so they are an admissible countable delta-cover of E. Its s-cost is at most sum_i rho_i^s*1_{J_i}(t)=sum_i f_i(t). The definition of c as an infimum gives c<=sum_i f_i(t) for every t in I.

argument.text:
Integrate F003 against lambda restricted to I. Since lambda(I)=1, the integral of the finite constant c is c. Apply M001 with X=R, K the countable subset of N above, mu=lambda restricted to I, and the nonnegative measurable family f from F002. It gives integral_I sum_i f_i = sum_i integral_I f_i. For each i, integration of its indicator times the constant gives integral_I f_i=rho_i^s*lambda(J_i intersect I). Thus, using F002,
c <= sum_i rho_i^s*lambda(J_i intersect I) <= sum_i rho_i^s*(rho_i+eta_i) = sum_i rho_i^(s+1)+sum_i eta_i*rho_i^s <= sum_i rho_i^(s+1)+epsilon.
The last bound follows termwise from eta_i*rho_i^s=epsilon*2^(-i-1)*rho_i^s/(1+rho_i^s)<=epsilon*2^(-i-1) and sum_{i in K}2^(-i-1)<=1. All inequalities are valid for nonnegative extended sums. If the cost sum_i rho_i^(s+1) is infinite, c<=that cost immediately. Otherwise the cost and c are finite, and since this estimate is available for every epsilon>0, let epsilon decrease to zero to obtain c<=sum_i rho_i^(s+1). The interval enlargement did not alter V, rho or c, so the limit keeps the original arbitrary cover fixed.

produces.statement: For the arbitrary delta-cover V of F, H^s_delta(E)=c<=sum_{i in K} rho_i^(s+1), where rho_i=diam(V_i); empty members contribute zero.

argument.text: Every countable delta-cover V of F was arbitrary in this argument. F004 bounds c by each of its (s+1)-costs, so taking their infimum gives H^s_delta(E)<=H^(s+1)_delta(F). The positive exponent s and scale delta were arbitrary. This proves the content inequality on their full stated domains, including n=0 and without any measurability assumption on cover members or their projections.

applications.bindings: Set the source type X=R with its Lebesgue measurable space, index type K={i in N:V_i nonempty}, measure mu=lambda restricted to I, and source family f(i,t)=rho_i^s*1_{J_i}(t), valued in [0,infinity].
hypothesis_checks: Lebesgue length lambda is a measure; its restriction to the measurable closed interval I is a measure on the same measurable space.
K is a subset of N and therefore countable, as recorded in F002.

F002 proves each J_i open and each coefficient finite and nonnegative, so its indicator multiple is measurable for Lebesgue measure and therefore almost everywhere measurable for the restricted measure.

locals.declaration: Under D>0 fix an arbitrary s with 0<s<D.

argument.text: Assume L1: D>0. N002 gives D finite. Fix any 0<s<D. N001 gives H^s(E)=infinity. By definition H^s(E)=sup_{delta>0} H^s_delta(E); contents increase when the scale decreases, because fewer covers are admissible. Thus the left contents become arbitrarily large as delta decreases to zero: for any finite threshold choose one scale exceeding it, and all smaller scales also exceed it. N005 gives H^s_delta(E)<=H^(s+1)_delta(F) at each scale. Taking the supremum over scales therefore gives H^(s+1)(F)=infinity. Since s+1>0, N001 gives dim_H(F)>=s+1.

produces.statement: Under D>0, for every real s_b with 0<s_b<D, H^(s_b+1)(F)=infinity and dim_H(F)>=s_b+1.

argument.text: Use F001 for s increasing to D from below, possible because 0<D<infinity by N002 (for example s=D*(1-1/k) for integers k>=2). Then s+1 increases to D+1. The inequalities dim_H(F)>=s+1 imply dim_H(F)>=D+1, also if dim_H(F) is infinite. Discharge L1 and retain exactly the implication D>0 -> dim_H(F)>=D+1.

locals.declaration: Choose x0 in E using H001.
Define j(t)=(x0,t), whose image is contained in F.
Fix any 0<s<1.

argument.text: Assume L1: D=0. Nonemptiness H001 supplies a point of E. We will compare the copy of I above that point directly by covers, which proves the required instance of dimension monotonicity and isometry invariance without importing a further dimension theorem.

Choose x0 in E by H001 and define j:I->F by j(t)=(x0,t). Euclidean distance satisfies dist(j(t),j(u))=|t-u|, so j is an isometric embedding, including when n=0. For an arbitrary positive scale delta and any countable delta-cover V of F, its preimages {t in I:j(t) in V_i} cover I and have diameters no larger than diam(V_i), by the displayed distance equality. Thus H^s_delta(I)<=H^s_delta(F) for every s>0 and delta>0. Taking supremums over scales gives H^s(I)<=H^s(F). In particular for 0<s<1, N003 gives H^s(I)=infinity, so H^s(F)=infinity.

By N001 and F001, dim_H(F)>=s for every 0<s<1, so letting s increase to 1 gives dim_H(F)>=1. Under L1, 1=D+1. The construction used only a point x0 of E and the Euclidean product distance, so it includes n=0. Discharge L1 to obtain the claimed conditional lower bound.

N002 gives 0<=D<=n, hence D is a finite nonnegative real. Its exhaustive alternatives are D>0 or D=0. In the first alternative N006 yields dim_H(F)>=D+1; in the second N007 yields the same bound. N004 supplies dim_H(F)<=D+1 in both cases. Antisymmetry gives dim_H(F)=D+1. Substitute F=E x I, I=[0,1], D=dim_H(E) and the Euclidean coordinate identification from D001. This is dim_H(E x [0,1])=dim_H(E)+1 for the complete original nonnegative integer ambient range, including n=0.
